study_identification_part.si4_title: Mapping the Heterogeneous Brain Structural Phenotype of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using the Normative Model

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To develop a parameterized, low-dimensional, and individualized metric to delineate heterogeneity of brain structure in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) by combining non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) and normative modeling to identify homogeneous subgroups with distinct clinical phenotypes.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Two-sample t-tests and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests with FDR correction for group comparisons (ASD vs TD) of weights and deviations; Pearson correlation analysis with Bonferroni correction (p < .05/18) between residual weights and ADOS clinical scores (communication, social, RRB); Gaussian mixture clustering to identify ASD subtypes based on deviation matrix; One-way ANOVA and chi-square tests to compare demographic and clinical characteristics across subtypes; covariates (age, gender, handedness, FSIQ, sites) regressed out using generalized linear model (GLM) prior to group comparisons
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Three distinct neuroanatomical ASD subtypes were identified with heterogeneous deviation patterns from normative brain structure, showing significant differences in social communication deficits but not in restricted/repetitive behaviors, suggesting that distinct gray matter patterns relate to core ASD symptoms.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Compared to TD, ASD showed significantly increased weights and deviations in 5 of 6 factors (factors 1, 3, 4, 5, 6; p < .05 FDR-corrected), indicating larger gray matter volume in corresponding brain regions including medial cortex, occipital lobe/inferior parietal lobule/thalamus, parietal lobe, frontal lobe, and limbic system. Three ASD subtypes were identified: subtype 1 (n=143, all positive deviations ranging 0-0.5), subtype 2 (n=76, all negative deviations, higher proportion of females), and subtype 3 (n=53, all positive deviations >0.5). Significant between-subtype differences were found in ADOS communication scores (subtypes 1 vs 2: pFDR = .003; subtypes 2 vs 3: pFDR = .020) and ADOS social scores (subtypes 1 vs 2: pFDR = .013; subtypes 2 vs 3: pFDR = .008), with subtype 2 showing the lowest scores. No significant differences in ADOS RRB scores were observed across subtypes. Factor weights correlated with clinical symptoms: factors 1 and 4 correlated with ADOS communication (r = 0.185, p = .002; r = 0.181, p = .0028); factors 2, 4, 5, 6 correlated with ADOS social scores (r = 0.210-0.217, p < .001, Bonferroni corrected). Reproducibility analysis using reverse validation (ABIDE I TD normative model applied to ABIDE II ASD) yielded similar results with three subtypes and comparable clinical symptom differences, with Dice coefficient of 0.530 indicating stability of clustering solution.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Only age and gender considered as covariates in normative model; cognitive scores and home environment not included; no brain-symptom correlations found within or across subtypes; other modalities (resting-state fMRI, diffusion tensor imaging, genetic data) not incorporated
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: Our study has several limitations. First, only age and gender were considered as independent variables to estimate the brain readout in the normative model. Cognitive scores and home environment may also affect the brain index. These covariates also need to be considered for more comprehensive models. Second, although we demonstrated the stability and robustness of the clustering solution in different datasets, we did not find any brain-symptom correlations either within or across subtypes... Finally, other modalities, including resting-state functional MRI, diffusion tensor imaging, and genetic data, need to be incorporated to parse the heterogeneity of ASD.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: Non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) used for dimensionality reduction of voxelwise gray matter maps into 6 interpretable latent factors before normative modeling; back-reconstruction NMF algorithm applied to obtain weights for new subjects from fixed factor matrix; meta-analytic decoding via NeuroSynth used to interpret functional associations of each factor (26 terms); sparsity parameter (lambda = 0.3) and number of factors (K = 6) optimized based on reconstruction error and reproducibility across ABIDE I and II TD cohorts; Gaussian mixture clustering with Calinski Harabasz score and Silhouette score used to determine optimal number of subtypes (K = 3)

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This study employed a two-stage approach: (1) NMF decomposition to reduce high-dimensional voxelwise gray matter data into 6 low-dimensional latent factors and corresponding weights, then (2) normative modeling using GPR to predict these weights from age and gender. The approach differs from typical voxelwise or ROI-wise normative modeling by operating on data-driven latent features. Site information from ABIDE datasets: ABIDE II includes 19 sites, many of which are new or represent newly collected data from sites that participated in ABIDE I (see supplementary Table S6 for detailed site relationships). The study demonstrates bidirectional validation: ABIDE II TD → ABIDE I ASD (main analysis) and ABIDE I TD → ABIDE II ASD (reproducibility analysis). Age range is very broad (5.8-64 years for normative cohort, 7-64 years for ASD), spanning childhood through older adulthood. The paper emphasizes that the neurobiological heterogeneity identified may help explain inconsistent findings in the ASD literature and could guide precision medicine approaches.
